text: The last two lessons leaned on --query and plain-text output to pull one or two fields out of az and aws responses. That works fine for a single value, but it starts to strain fast once a script needs several fields, a filter condition, or a reshaped result. This lesson introduces jq — a command-line tool built specifically to query and reshape JSON, usable with either cloud's CLI.

Both az and aws can emit raw JSON with --output json — az's own default is already JSON. Piped into jq, that response stays JSON the whole way through instead of becoming a long, increasingly fragile --query string crammed into one command-line argument, or a pile of grep and cut commands trying to scrape structured data apart as if it were plain text.

jq's core pieces are small. The dot by itself is the identity filter, printing input unchanged. Dot-bracket-bracket iterates over every element of an array. Adding dot-name after it pulls that field from each element. The dash-r flag prints raw text instead of wrapping string values in quotes.

select() filters a response down to only the elements matching a condition. aws ec2 describe-instances piped into jq with select where State.Name equals running, then InstanceId, returns just the running instances' IDs — one aws call, one filter, no per-instance loop required the way Lesson 14's script needed.

jq can also combine fields into one readable line with string interpolation: backslash-parentheses around a field name drops its value straight into a formatted string, so az vm list piped through a jq filter with name and location together prints something like web-vm-01 (eastus) in a single pass.

Between --query for simple single-field pulls and jq for anything more involved — filtering, combining fields, reshaping a response — a script now has a clean way to handle whatever shape of JSON either cloud hands back. Next up: putting az, aws, and jq together into one real multi-cloud report.
